newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NYSE SEES CHALLENGE TO EXCHANGES FROM INTERNET.
newsitem.headline: NYSE SEES CHALLENGE TO EXCHANGES FROM INTERNET.

text.p: Trade in shares in the world's top corporations will increasingly move away from organised stock exchanges to off-market systems, such as the Internet, unless the exchanges react, a top New York Stock Exchange executive said on Wednesday.

"The New York Stock Exchange is 205-years-old...but we have no God given right to make it to 207. To exist in the medium-term we have to figure a way to get into the nitches which we believe are the way the business is developing," NYSE Senior Vice President (Research) James Cochrane told a conference on global accounting standards.

Cochrane said the top three thousand companies in the world were likely to increasingly adopt common disclosure and reporting standards as they became available, facilitating cross-border listings and comparison of businesses.

While regulation of the markets would essentially remain national, because of the problem of agreeing on common judicial systems and prosecuting fraudsters, trading would become global, he said, citing three main trends.
First, increasing adaptation of companies' home market exchanges to 24-hour, seven-day a week global markets by extending hours in order to keep business in key blue chips.
Second, stock brokerages passing their equity positions around the world's time zones in the same way that banks do now with their foreign exchange and U.S. Treasury "books".

U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch's 1995 purchase of British stock brokerage Smith Newcourt Plc was an example of securities companies positioning themselves for such round-the-clock equity trading, he said.
Third, a combination of global information vendors and proprietary networks, drawing business away from bourses.
He said he meant by this the trend for retail investors to increasingly turn to the Internet for their financial information and investment advice.

Standards played a role in this, he said, noting some companies, such as Microsoft , already offer investors a choice of viewing their figures on their web sites according to various national accounting practices.

Some large securities houses were also opting for closed networks outside organised markets for transactions, noting 22 U.S. trading houses already had an end-of-day arrangement whereby they squared positions. He did not cite the names of the companies concerned.
